title: Disaggregated prefill and decode
summary: Why prefill and decode interfere, how goodput under TTFT and TPOT SLOs is measured and simulated, what moving the KV cache costs and how the handoff works, and when splitting phases wins, up to MoE scale.
outcomes: Explain why mixing compute-bound prefill with memory-bound decode inflates TTFT and TPOT on a shared GPU
Compute SLO attainment and per-GPU goodput from a rate sweep, and build a discrete-event simulator that finds goodput
Compute KV transfer time from model config, prompt length and link bandwidth, and check sustained bandwidth
Trace a KV handoff through a pull connector, including leases, heterogeneous TP layouts and failure policies
Explain how DistServe, Splitwise and Mooncake size, place and connect prefill and decode pools

lessons.title: Why prefill stalls decode on a shared GPU

blocks.md:
Recall from the KV cache course: a request runs in two phases. **Prefill** pushes the whole prompt through the model in one forward pass, writes every prompt token's keys and values into the KV cache, and produces the first output token. **Decode** then generates one token per step, reading the whole KV cache each time.

The two phases use the GPU very differently. A step is *compute-bound* when its time is set by how fast the GPU's arithmetic units can do the math, and *memory-bandwidth-bound* when it is set by how fast bytes stream in from GPU memory while the arithmetic waits. A prefill of a few hundred tokens or more is compute-bound: DistServe, the 2024 research system this course follows most closely, reports that a single 512-token prompt nearly saturates an NVIDIA A100 GPU for a 13B (13-billion-parameter) model. A decode step does almost the same weight reads as a prefill but only one token of math per request, so it is memory-bandwidth-bound.

Two latency numbers follow from the two phases. DistServe (Zhong et al., OSDI 2024, the USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation) defines:

- **TTFT** (time to first token): the time from arrival until prefill finishes and the first token appears.
- **TPOT** (time per output token): the average time per generated token after the first one.

Splitwise (another 2024 research system that splits the phases, lesson 3) calls the per-step gap **TBT** (time between tokens), Mooncake (the serving system behind Moonshot AI's Kimi chatbot) uses TBT too, and the docs of vLLM (the open-source engine from the KV cache course) say **ITL** (inter-token latency). TPOT is an average over a request; TBT and ITL are usually looked at per step, which makes a single long stall visible.

blocks.caption: The minus 1 is there because the first output token is already counted inside TTFT. Each phase controls one term. DistServe's footnote writes it with TPOT times the tokens generated in the decoding phase.

blocks.md: Modern engines use **continuous batching**: every iteration, the scheduler mixes the prefill of newly arrived prompts with one decode step of every running request. That keeps the GPU busy, but now both phases share one iteration time.

The figure uses a simplified cost model taken from the **roofline** view in Sarathi-Serve (a scheduler covered in lesson 6): the GPU does math and memory reads at the same time, so a step takes as long as the slower of the two, $T=\max(T_{math}, T_{mem})$. Here an iteration costs $\max(15 + 0.2B,\ 0.1(P+B))$ ms for $P$ prefill tokens and $B$ decoding requests. Read the memory side as 15 ms to stream the weights once plus 0.2 ms per running request to read its KV cache, and the math side as 0.1 ms per token processed, where each decoding request adds one token. The constants are made up for illustration, not measured.

blocks.title: One prompt arrives while 16 requests are decoding

scenes.caption: 16 requests are decoding. Each step costs max(15 + 0.2 x 16, 0.1 x 16) = 18.2 ms, so every running request gets a token every 18.2 ms. A new 1024-token prompt C arrives at t = 30 ms.
The next iteration carries C's whole prefill plus the 16 decode steps: max(18.2, 0.1 x 1040) = 104 ms. Every running request waits 104 ms for its next token instead of 18.2 ms.
C's first token appears at 140.4 ms, so its TTFT is 110.4 ms (6.4 ms queueing plus 104 ms of work). Decoding resumes with 17 requests at 18.4 ms per step. One prompt cost 16 users a 5.7x longer gap.

blocks.md:
This is **prefill-decode interference**, and it goes both ways. DistServe measured that adding one prefill to a decode batch slows the decodes (longer TPOT), and the slowdown grows with prompt length. Adding decode work to a prefill also stretches it (longer TTFT) once the GPU is saturated.

Scheduling the phases in separate iterations does not fix it either: decodes then queue behind prefills, and prioritizing one phase hurts the other.

blocks.prompt: DistServe served a 13B model (prompts of 512 tokens, 64 output tokens) on one A100 and found about 1.6 requests/s within both latency targets. A prefill-only GPU sustained 5.6 req/s and a decode-only GPU 10 req/s. What per-GPU rate could 2 prefill GPUs plus 1 decode GPU reach?
blocks.reveal: Two prefill GPUs give 2 x 5.6 = 11.2 req/s of prefill capacity, so the single decode GPU (10 req/s) becomes the limit: **10 req/s over 3 GPUs, about 3.3 req/s per GPU**. That is roughly 2.1x the colocated 1.6 req/s, from the same hardware, just by not making the phases share a GPU. This back-of-envelope example in the DistServe introduction is the whole idea of disaggregation in one line.

blocks.md: There is a second, quieter problem: **coupled resources**. When both phases share GPUs they must share one parallelism plan and one GPU count, sized for whichever latency target is harder. Prefill wants more tensor parallelism (each layer's matrices split across several GPUs, so one prompt's math runs on all of them at once) to cut TTFT; decode's best plan depends on its batch size. DistServe argues that colocated systems end up over-provisioning to satisfy both.

Misconception: "interference only matters at high load." In the timeline there was just one new prompt. Any long prompt that lands in a decode iteration creates a stall for every request in the batch. Load makes it more frequent, not possible.
Prefill is compute-bound and sets TTFT; decode is memory-bound and sets TPOT. Putting both in one batch makes each phase pay for the other.

blocks.question: In the toy model, a decode step for 16 requests costs 18.2 ms. A 4096-token prompt would join the next iteration in full. Roughly how long would the 16 running requests wait for their next token?
options: About 18 ms, because decode is memory-bound and unaffected
About 104 ms, the same as for a 1024-token prompt
About 36 ms, two decode steps
About 411 ms, because the iteration now costs max(18.2, 0.1 x 4112)
blocks.explain: The iteration time is set by the slower of math and memory. 4096 prompt tokens plus 16 decode tokens is 4112 tokens of math, 0.1 x 4112 = 411.2 ms, which dominates 18.2 ms. The stall scales with prompt length, which is exactly what DistServe's Figure 2 shows.

blocks.question: Which metric does a chat user notice first if prefills are always scheduled ahead of decodes on a busy colocated GPU?
options: Neither, since prefill priority helps everyone
Throughput in tokens per second must drop
TTFT gets worse
TPOT/TBT gets worse: running streams stutter while new prompts are processed
blocks.explain: Prioritizing prefill keeps TTFT low but every prefill iteration delays the next token of every running request. Splitwise notes that letting a waiting prompt preempt token generation shortens TTFT but can substantially increase the tail of TBT. Throughput may even rise; latency of the other phase is what suffers.

lessons.title: Goodput: requests per GPU that meet both SLOs

blocks.md:
Raw throughput (tokens or requests per second) rewards a server that keeps the GPU full, even if half the users stare at a frozen stream. DistServe instead optimizes **goodput**: the highest request rate a deployment can sustain while a target fraction of requests meet *both* latency targets.

The targets are **SLOs** (service level objectives), such as TTFT at most 400 ms and TPOT at most 25 ms. **SLO attainment** is the fraction of requests that meet all of them. DistServe's experiments use a 90% attainment goal (and report 99% in an appendix).

blocks.caption: In words: find the largest arrival rate lambda (requests per second) at which at least 90% of requests meet both TTFT at most T1 and TPOT at most T2, then divide by the GPU count N. Dividing makes a 3-GPU design comparable with a 1-GPU design, so it maps to cost per query.

blocks.md: Start with a tiny example. Eight requests were served (made-up measurements) with SLOs TTFT at most 400 ms and TPOT at most 25 ms. A request counts only if it meets both.

scenes.caption: The raw measurements. The SLOs are TTFT at most 400 ms and TPOT at most 25 ms.
Check TTFT: the requests at index 3 and 6 are too slow (450 and 520 ms). TTFT attainment alone is 6/8 = 75%.
Check TPOT: the request at index 4 streams too slowly (31 ms per token). TPOT attainment alone is 7/8 = 87.5%.
Joint attainment counts requests that pass both: 5/8 = 62.5%. That is below 90%, so this rate is above the goodput of the deployment, even though each metric alone looks decent.

blocks.md:
To find goodput you sweep the arrival rate, measure attainment at each rate, and take the largest rate still at or above 90%. DistServe does this with a simulator fitted to the model's prefill and decode latency (its paper reports under 2% error against real runs) and binary search, because testing every configuration on real GPUs is too slow.

The figure below comes from a toy discrete-event simulation run for this course (a program that jumps from one event, such as an arrival or the end of an iteration, to the next). It uses **Poisson arrivals**, meaning requests arrive independently at random at a fixed average rate, like many unrelated users; every prompt is 1024 tokens, with 128 output tokens, SLOs of 400 ms TTFT and 25 ms TPOT, and the same made-up iteration cost as lesson 1. The rates are *per GPU*, so the 3-GPU disaggregated setup is offered three times the total traffic.

blocks.title: Toy simulation: SLO attainment vs per-GPU request rate

scenes.caption: One colocated GPU with full prefills mixed into decode batches. Attainment is 90% at 2.5 req/s and falls fast after it, mostly from TPOT misses caused by prefill stalls. Its goodput is 2.50 req/s.
Two prefill GPUs plus one decode GPU (2P1D), offered three times the traffic. It stays at or above 90% up to about 4.5 req/s per GPU (13.5 req/s in total), so per-GPU goodput is 4.51.

blocks.md: Goodput is not throughput. A colocated GPU at 4 req/s still produces plenty of tokens per second, but in the toy run only 28% of requests meet both SLOs. If you only tracked throughput, that overloaded point would look like the best one.

Here is the whole simulator behind those bars, about 70 lines of plain Python that run on any laptop. Its core is one function, `gpu()`, that plays a single GPU running continuous batching. A job is a list: ready time, prompt tokens still to prefill, decode steps left. Every iteration admits the jobs that have arrived, runs one decode step for each running job, fills the rest of an optional token budget with prefill tokens first come first served (no budget means whole prompts), and advances the clock by lesson 1's cost $\max(15 + 0.2B,\ 0.1(P + B))$ ms. A job whose prompt finishes gets its first token; a job that arrives with nothing to prefill, because its KV came from elsewhere, goes straight to decoding.

blocks.caption: goodput_sim.py: one GPU with continuous batching and lesson 1's toy cost. The same engine plays a colocated GPU, a prefill GPU (jobs with 0 decode steps) or a decode GPU (jobs with 0 prompt tokens left).

blocks.md: The deployments are built from that one engine. `colocated` feeds every request to one GPU. `disagg` sends requests round-robin to nP prefill GPUs whose jobs have no decode steps, then hands each finished prompt, after an optional KV transfer delay `xfer`, to one of nD decode GPUs as a job with nothing left to prefill. TTFT ends when prefill finishes, as in DistServe (in vLLM's proxy flow, lesson 5, the decoder streams the first token, so the client's TTFT also includes the transfer and the decoder's queue). TPOT is measured from the first token, so waiting for the transfer and for a decode slot counts against it. `attainment` drops the first 10% of requests as warm-up (the queue starts empty), and `goodput` binary-searches the per-GPU rate at which joint attainment crosses 90%.

blocks.code:
from goodput_sim import *

def arrivals(rate, n=2000, seed=0):            # Poisson: exponential gaps
    rng, t = random.Random(seed), 0.0
    return [t := t + rng.expovariate(rate) for _ in range(n)]

def colocated(rate, budget=None):              # one GPU does everything
    arr = arrivals(rate)
    f, e = gpu([[a, PROMPT, OUT - 1] for a in arr], budget)
    return [(f[i] - a, (e[i] - f[i]) / (OUT - 1)) for i, a in enumerate(arr)]

def disagg(rate, nP, nD, xfer=0.0):            # rate is per GPU
    arr = arrivals(rate * (nP + nD))
    first, end = {}, {}
    for g in range(nP):                        # round-robin prefill GPUs
        ids = range(g, len(arr), nP)
        f, _ = gpu([[arr[i], PROMPT, 0] for i in ids])
        first.update({i: f[j] for j, i in enumerate(ids)})
    for g in range(nD):                        # KV arrives, decode only
        ids = range(g, len(arr), nD)
        _, e = gpu([[first[i] + xfer, 0, OUT - 1] for i in ids])
        end.update({i: e[j] for j, i in enumerate(ids)})
    return [(first[i] - a, (end[i] - first[i]) / (OUT - 1))
            for i, a in enumerate(arr)]

def attainment(res):                           # both SLOs, after warm-up
    res = res[len(res) // 10:]
    return sum(t <= SLO_TTFT and p <= SLO_TPOT for t, p in res) / len(res)

def goodput(design, lo=0.1, hi=20.0):          # binary search on the rate
    for _ in range(25):
        mid = (lo + hi) / 2
        lo, hi = (mid, hi) if attainment(design(mid)) >= 0.9 else (lo, mid)
    return lo
blocks.caption: designs.py: colocated and disaggregated deployments, joint SLO attainment, and the goodput search. Every run uses 2,000 Poisson arrivals from a fixed seed, so results repeat exactly.

blocks.md:
The toy cost is not special. With the GPU course's step model the decode step never drops below 7.85 ms, the time to read 16 GB of weights at 2.039 TB/s, and a step that carries a 1,024-token prefill takes about 52.5 ms, since its math then outweighs the weight reads. Output:

```
TPOT SLO 25 ms: colocated 12.0, chunk 512 14.4, 2P1D 11.3
TPOT SLO 15 ms: colocated 7.9, chunk 512 10.1, 2P1D 11.3
TPOT SLO 10 ms: colocated 3.0, chunk 512 3.7, 2P1D 11.3
```

Same story in this simulator: chunking wins while the TPOT budget leaves room for prefill tokens, and as TPOT nears the 7.85 ms floor only a GPU that never prefills keeps it. Real planners use the same loop with measured costs. DistServe fits its simulator from profiling and reports under 2% error; **Vidur** (Agrawal et al., 2024) profiles each operator, reports under 9% latency error, and its Vidur-Search found a deployment for LLaMA2-70B in one hour on a CPU machine instead of an estimated 42K GPU hours.

Real SLOs depend on the application. DistServe set them per workload: a chatbot on OPT-13B (OPT, Open Pre-trained Transformer, is Meta's open model family; the number is the parameter count) used 0.25 s TTFT and 0.1 s TPOT; code completion on OPT-66B used a tight 0.125 s TTFT; summarization of long documents used a loose 15 s TTFT but a 0.15 s TPOT. Tight TTFT pushes resources toward prefill; tight TPOT pushes them toward decode. Mooncake frames the same goal as maximizing throughput under TTFT and TBT SLOs, and counts only requests that fully complete.
Goodput = the highest rate at which at least 90% (or your target) of requests meet every latency SLO, divided by the GPUs used. It is the number disaggregation is designed to raise.

blocks.question: System A serves 9 req/s on 3 GPUs at 92% attainment. System B serves 4 req/s on 1 GPU at 91% attainment, and 4.5 req/s at 85%. Assuming these are the largest rates meeting 90%, which has higher per-GPU goodput?
options: They tie, since both exceed 90%
A, because 9 req/s is more than 4 req/s
B, with 4 req/s per GPU against A's 3
B, with 4.5 req/s per GPU
blocks.explain: Per-GPU goodput divides the highest rate meeting the attainment goal by the GPU count: A gives 9/3 = 3 req/s per GPU and B gives 4/1 = 4. B's 4.5 req/s point misses the 90% goal, so it does not count.

blocks.question: Your summarization service has a 15 s TTFT SLO and a 0.15 s TPOT SLO. Attainment is failing. Which change most likely helps?
options: Protect decode steps from long prefills (separate decode GPUs or smaller prefill chunks)
Give prefill more tensor parallelism to cut TTFT
Lower the TTFT SLO to 5 s
Batch more prompts into each prefill
blocks.explain: With a 15 s TTFT budget, prefill is rarely the binding constraint. The long documents create long prefills that stall decode steps and break the TPOT SLO, which DistServe observed for vLLM on LongBench, a benchmark of long-document tasks. Shielding decode is the fix; batching more prompts would make the stalls worse.

lessons.title: Splitting the phases: pools, ratios and parallelism

blocks.md: Disaggregation gives each phase its own GPUs. DistServe calls a unit that holds one full copy of the weights an **instance** (one GPU, or several when model parallelism splits the model across GPUs). A **prefill instance** only runs prompts and produces the first token; a **decode instance** receives the request's KV cache and generates the rest. Splitwise (Patel et al., ISCA 2024, the International Symposium on Computer Architecture) builds the same split from machine pools and calls the phases *prompt* and *token*.

blocks.title: A request through a disaggregated deployment

scenes.caption: Two prefill instances feed one decode instance, the 2:1 ratio from DistServe's introduction. The pools are sized separately.
DistServe's controller sends each new request to the prefill instance with the shortest queue. Prefill computes the prompt's KV cache and the first token.
The KV cache moves to the least-loaded decode instance. In DistServe the decode side pulls it when it has room, so the prefill GPU's memory acts as the queue during bursts.
The decode instance adds the request to its continuous batch and streams tokens. It never runs a prefill, so its steps stay short and steady.

blocks.md: Once the phases are apart, each can be tuned for its own SLO. DistServe analyzes a prefill instance as an **M/D/1 queue**, queueing-theory shorthand: M (memoryless) means Poisson arrivals at rate $R$, D (deterministic) means every prompt takes the same service time $D$, and 1 means one server. The server is busy a fraction $RD$ of the time. A classic result for this queue, the Pollaczek-Khinchine formula, puts the average wait at $RD^2/(2(1-RD))$: the arrival rate times the square of the service time, divided by twice the idle fraction $1-RD$, so it blows up as $RD$ nears 1. Average TTFT is that wait plus the execution time $D$.

Why the 2, and why does $1 - RD$ matter so much? The general Pollaczek-Khinchine formula is $W = R\,E[S^2]/(2(1-RD))$, where $E[S^2]$ is the mean squared service time. A new request waits for the rest of the request in service plus the queue, and it is more likely to land during a long service than a short one, so variable service hurts. Deterministic service has $E[S^2] = D^2$; exponential service (the M/M/1 queue) has $E[S^2] = 2D^2$, so M/M/1 waits exactly twice as long. With $D = 0.1$ s: at $RD = 0.5$ the M/D/1 wait is 0.05 s (M/M/1: 0.1 s); at $RD = 0.9$ it is 0.45 s (M/M/1: 0.9 s). Going from half busy to 90% busy multiplies the wait by 9: $R$ itself grows 1.8x (5 to 9 req/s) and $1 - RD$ shrinks 5x, from 0.5 to 0.1. The *Tail latency* course (not a prerequisite) covers queueing and the utilization knee in depth.

It then compares two ways to use 2 GPUs. **Inter-op** (inter-operator, or pipeline) parallelism puts different layers on each GPU: a request still takes about $D$ in total, but each stage is busy only $D/2$ per request, so capacity doubles and $D/2$ goes into the wait formula. **Intra-op** (intra-operator, or tensor) parallelism splits every layer's math across both GPUs, cutting the time to $D/K$ for a speedup $1 < K < 2$ lost partly to communication, and $D/K$ goes into the wait formula. Substituting gives the three equations below.

blocks.caption: DistServe equations 1 to 3, for one GPU, 2-way pipeline and 2-way tensor. First term: execution time. Second term: queueing delay, which explodes as the server nears full utilization.

blocks.title: Prefill TTFT on 2 GPUs: pipeline vs tensor parallelism

scenes.caption: D = 0.1 s, K = 1.6. At low rates tensor parallelism wins (0.067 s vs 0.103 s at R = 2) because execution time dominates. Past about 11 req/s pipeline wins because queueing dominates.
With a better speedup K = 1.9, tensor parallelism stays ahead over the plotted range. A tight TTFT SLO or fast interconnect favors intra-op; DistServe searches this space automatically.

blocks.md: DistServe turns this into a placement search. For each phase it enumerates parallelism configurations, uses its simulator to find the highest rate meeting the SLO attainment target, keeps the best per-GPU goodput, and then replicates instances to match the traffic. For OPT-175B on ShareGPT (a dataset of real ChatGPT conversations that users shared publicly) it chose prefill with inter-op 3 and intra-op 3 (3 pipeline stages, each split across 3 GPUs), and decode with inter-op 3 and intra-op 4, a plan a human would rarely guess. The search took under 1.3 minutes in their largest setting.

blocks.title: Toy simulation: per-GPU goodput by pool ratio

scenes.caption: Same toy workload as lesson 2, from its simulator. Colocated: 2.50 req/s per GPU. A 1:1 split reaches 6.1 req/s on 2 GPUs, only 3.05 per GPU, because the prefill GPU limits TTFT while the decode GPU sits partly idle.

2P1D reaches 13.5 req/s on 3 GPUs (4.51 per GPU). 3P1D adds a GPU but the decode GPU becomes the limit: 13.7 req/s on 4 GPUs, 3.42 per GPU. 3P2D gives 25.6 on 5, 5.12 per GPU. The ratio matters as much as the split.

blocks.md: Splitwise adds a hardware angle. Its characterization on Azure production traces found that token generation barely uses the compute of the newest GPUs: with power capped by half (700 W to 350 W per H100, NVIDIA's generation after the A100), the token phase saw almost no latency impact while the prompt phase slowed a lot. So Splitwise-HA uses H100 machines for prompts and A100 machines for tokens (H for H100, A for A100), and Splitwise-HHcap uses H100s for both but power-caps the token machines. The paper reports up to 1.4x higher throughput at 20% lower cost, or 2.35x more throughput for the same cost and power budget.

Splitwise also keeps a **mixed pool**: machines borrowed from the prompt or token pool run both phases with mixed batching when load shifts, then return to their pool. This softens the fragmentation that a fixed prefill:decode ratio would otherwise cause.

blocks.question: A disaggregated deployment meets TTFT easily but misses TPOT at high load, and decode GPUs are near their KV memory limit. What is the most sensible next change?
options: Increase the prefill batch size
Merge the pools back into a colocated deployment
Add prefill instances
Add decode capacity (more decode instances or more parallelism per decode instance)
blocks.explain: TPOT is decided by the decode side. Decode batch size is bounded by KV memory, and DistServe notes that scaling the decoding instance with model parallelism (or memory techniques like PagedAttention and GQA) lets it batch more. Extra prefill instances would just send more KV caches to an already full decode pool.

blocks.question: Using DistServe's equations with D = 0.1 s and K = 1.6, which 2-GPU plan gives lower average TTFT at a low arrival rate of 2 req/s?
options: Intra-op (tensor): it cuts execution time to D/K, and queueing is small at low rate
Neither; one GPU is always better
Inter-op (pipeline): it doubles capacity
They are identical at low rate
blocks.explain: At R = 2 the intra-op TTFT is 0.0625 + 0.0045 = about 0.067 s, while inter-op is 0.1 + 0.0028 = about 0.103 s. Execution time dominates at low load, so cutting it wins. At high load the queueing term flips the order.

lessons.title: Moving the KV cache: bytes, links and overlap

blocks.md: Disaggregation's price is that the KV cache built by prefill must reach the decode GPU before the second token. Splitwise calls this transfer the main overhead of the design. How big is it? From the KV cache course, each token stores one key and one value vector per layer per KV head. So bytes per token is 2 (one key and one value) times layers times KV heads times head size times bytes per number, and an ideal transfer takes prompt tokens times bytes per token divided by link bandwidth.

blocks.tex: \text{bytes/token} = 2 \times L \times H_{kv} \times d_{head} \times b,\qquad t_{transfer} = \frac{\text{prompt tokens} \times \text{bytes/token}}{\text{link bandwidth}}
blocks.caption: L layers, H_kv key/value heads, d_head head size, b bytes per element (2 for BF16 or FP16). Real transfers add setup and protocol overhead, so this is a lower bound.

blocks.md:
Units first: KiB is 1024 bytes and GiB is $2^{30}$ bytes, while GB means $10^9$ bytes. Link speeds are quoted in gigabits per second (Gb/s), so divide by 8 for gigabytes per second.

Worked example with Qwen3-32B, whose published config has 64 layers, 8 KV heads (grouped-query attention) and head size 128, stored in BF16:

- bytes per token: $2 \times 64 \times 8 \times 128 \times 2 = 262{,}144$ B = 256 KiB
- an 8192-token prompt: $8192 \times 262{,}144 = 2{,}147{,}483{,}648$ B = 2 GiB (about 2.15 GB)

Over three links, ignoring overhead: 25 Gb/s Ethernet, the ordinary data-center network (3.125 GB/s), takes 687 ms; a 400 Gb/s InfiniBand network card (50 GB/s) takes 43 ms, where InfiniBand is the low-latency network common in GPU clusters; NVLink, NVIDIA's direct GPU-to-GPU link inside a server, at the 600 GB/s peak DistServe quotes for A100s takes 3.6 ms.

blocks.title: Ideal KV transfer time vs prompt length

scenes.caption: At 400 Gb/s an 8192-token Qwen3-32B prompt moves in 43 ms. OPT-66B uses full multi-head attention (72 KV heads of 128 in 64 layers), so the same prompt carries 9x more bytes.
At 25 Gb/s, DistServe's cross-node bandwidth, even Qwen3-32B needs 687 ms for 8192 tokens. Sending KV across such a link at full size would eat most of a typical TTFT budget.
At 1600 Gb/s the Qwen3-32B transfer for 8192 tokens drops to about 11 ms. Bandwidth, the model's KV layout, and prompt length decide whether the transfer matters.

blocks.md:
Check the formula against DistServe: OPT-66B has 64 layers and hidden size 9216, so a token takes $2 \times 64 \times 9216 \times 2 = 2{,}359{,}296$ B and a 512-token request takes 1.125 GiB, the paper's "approximately 1.13GB". At 10 requests per second that is 11.25 GiB/s, or 90 Gib/s of sustained bandwidth, the paper's 90 Gbps.

That gives two separate checks for any link: **latency** (does one transfer fit inside the TTFT and TPOT budgets?) and **throughput** (can the link sustain request rate times KV bytes?). A 400 Gb/s link moves at most about 23 Qwen3-32B 8K-token caches per second; a 25 Gb/s link about 1.5.

The latency check gets much easier with **layer-wise streaming**. Each layer's KV cache is final as soon as that layer's prefill finishes, so it can be sent while the next layers compute. Splitwise does exactly this for large prompts (serial transfer for small ones), and Mooncake streams each layer's KV to the decode node while prefill continues. The figure groups the 64 layers into 4 blocks of 16 for readability.

blocks.title: Serialized vs layer-wise transfer (8K prompt, 25 Gb/s)

scenes.caption: Serialized: prefill (estimated 1454 ms, see below) finishes, then the whole 2 GiB crosses the 25 Gb/s link in 687 ms. Decode cannot start until 2141 ms.
Layer-wise in 4 groups: each group's KV (172 ms) is sent while the next group computes (364 ms). Only the last group's send is exposed: decode can start at 1626 ms.

Per layer, the exposed tail shrinks to one layer's KV: 33.5 MB, about 10.7 ms at 25 Gb/s. Splitwise measured a near-constant non-overlapped time of about 8 ms (A100) and 5 ms (H100) with this optimization.

blocks.md: The prefill time in the figure is an estimate, not a measurement. A forward pass costs about 2 floating-point operations (FLOP) per parameter per token: each weight multiplies an input once and the product is added to a sum. Qwen3-32B has about 31.2B non-embedding parameters (the embedding table is a lookup, not a matrix multiply), so an 8192-token prefill needs about $2 \times 31.2\text{B} \times 8192 \approx 511$ TFLOP of matrix math, a TFLOP being $10^{12}$ FLOPs.

Attention adds work that grows with the square of the prompt. Scoring queries against keys and then mixing values are two matrix products, 4 FLOPs per token pair per query dimension, and causal masking (each token looks only backward) halves the pairs. The query width here is 8192, not the hidden size 5120: Qwen3-32B's config sets 64 query heads with `head_dim` 128 explicitly, so attention runs wider than the residual stream and the output projection maps 8192 back to 5120. With 64 layers that is $2 \times 8192^2 \times 8192 \times 64 \approx 70$ TFLOP (using 5120 by mistake gives about 44). At an assumed sustained 400 TFLOP/s the total of about 581 TFLOP takes about 1.45 s, or 22.7 ms per layer, longer than the 10.7 ms per-layer transfer, so the stream keeps up.

Overlap hides latency, not bandwidth. If two prefill GPUs share that 25 Gb/s link and each finishes an 8K prompt every 1.45 s, they produce about 1.4 caches/s against a link that sustains about 1.5. Add a third and the link becomes the bottleneck, however well transfers overlap.

Placement manages the bandwidth check. DistServe's testbed had NVLink inside each 8-GPU node but only 25 Gbps between nodes, so its algorithm for clusters with slow links between nodes (the paper's low node-affinity case) splits each instance into pipeline stages and puts the prefill and decode segments of the *same* stage in one node; KV for a layer then only moves over NVLink. Even for OPT-175B, transfer was under 0.1% of total latency and over 95% of requests waited less than 30 ms.

**Mooncake** makes the KV cache the center of the design. It pools the GPU cluster's underused CPU, DRAM and SSD resources into a disaggregated KV cache and moves blocks with an RDMA-based component (Messenger, open-sourced as the Mooncake Transfer Engine, the name the *KV cache offloading* course uses; RDMA lets a network card read or write another machine's memory without that machine's CPU). A global scheduler, Conductor, picks a prefill node and a decode node for every request. Mooncake reports up to 525% more throughput in simulated long-context cases and 75% more requests for Kimi on real workloads. The figure walks one request through it, with lesson 1's toy prefill cost.

blocks.title: Mooncake: one long request from Conductor to decode

scenes.caption: A 16K-token prompt arrives. Node A already caches its first 6K tokens but has 2 s of queued work; node B caches nothing and is idle. Conductor estimates TTFT on each node as queue time plus prefill of the uncached part.

At 0.1 ms per uncached token, A gives 2 + 1.02 = 3.02 s and B from scratch 1.64 s. Conductor also prices B fetching A's prefix: 6K tokens of Qwen3-32B KV at 400 Gb/s take 32 ms, so 1.06 s. It picks B and migrates the hot prefix.

Long prompts use chunked pipeline parallelism (CPP): prefill nodes act as pipeline stages and the prompt is cut into chunks (typically over 1,000 tokens), so nodes work on different chunks of one request at once. Only stage boundaries cross the network.

As each layer finishes, its KV streams to the decode node's CPU memory, the layer-wise transfer of the timeline above. Once all of it has arrived, the request joins the decode node's next continuous batch.

Conductor pre-selected the decode node by load, but the node's local scheduler re-checks the TBT SLO when the KV arrives and may reject the request, wasting the prefill. Early rejection moves the check before prefill, using the larger of the two pools' loads.

blocks.md: Rejecting on the decode pool's *current* load has its own failure: Mooncake saw prefill and decode loads swing in opposite phases, which lesson 7 explains, and moved to rejection based on *predicted* decode load. The store itself (tiers, eviction, reload versus recompute) belongs to the *KV cache offloading* course (not a prerequisite); here it matters as the place prefixes come from and KV goes to.

Today the transport is usually a library. **NIXL** (NVIDIA Inference Xfer Library) provides point-to-point transfers across GPU memory, CPU memory and storage through plug-in backends such as UCX (Unified Communication X, an open-source high-performance networking framework); NVIDIA Dynamo (NVIDIA's open-source distributed serving framework, lesson 6) and vLLM's `NixlConnector` use it.

blocks.md: Transfer cost = prompt tokens x bytes per token / bandwidth. Grouped-query attention, layer-wise streaming and placement on fast links make it small; slow links and long prompts at high rates make it the bottleneck.

blocks.question: Using the formula, how long does an ideal transfer of a 4096-token Qwen3-32B prompt (256 KiB per token) take over a 400 Gb/s link?
options: About 2.7 ms
About 21.5 ms
About 344 ms
About 172 ms
blocks.explain: 4096 x 262,144 B = 1,073,741,824 B (1 GiB). 400 Gb/s is 50 GB/s, so 1.074 GB / 50 GB/s = 21.5 ms. Half of the 43 ms needed for 8192 tokens, because KV size grows linearly with prompt length.

blocks.question: A team streams KV layer by layer, so per-request exposed transfer is only 10 ms. At peak, prefill GPUs produce 40 GB/s of KV, and the shared link carries 25 GB/s. What happens?
options: TTFT rises slightly but TPOT is unaffected
Decode GPUs simply run larger batches
Nothing, because overlap already hid the transfer
Transfers queue up without bound: the link cannot sustain the KV production rate, so decode starts slip further and prefill memory fills
blocks.explain: Overlap hides one transfer behind compute, but sustained bandwidth must still exceed rate x KV bytes. At 40 GB/s produced against 25 GB/s carried, the backlog grows. DistServe's 90 Gbps example is exactly this throughput check.

lessons.title: The KV handoff in detail: protocol, layouts and failures

blocks.md: Lesson 4 sized the KV transfer; this lesson opens the arrow between "prefill done" and "decode starts". Take one request on Llama 3 8B: a 2,048-token prompt at 128 KiB per token (the KV cache course's number) is 256 MiB of KV, which a paged cache with 16-token blocks stores as 128 blocks of 2 MiB. The prefill GPU has those blocks; the decode GPU has nothing. Three things must happen: the decoder learns where the blocks are, the bytes move, and the prefiller learns when it may reuse that memory. We follow vLLM's `NixlConnector`, the connector in lesson 4's launch command, because its docs and code spell out every step.

blocks.title: One request through vLLM's NixlConnector (pull mode)

scenes.caption: The proxy (toy_proxy_server.py in the docs) first sends the request to a prefiller with max_tokens set to 1 and kv_transfer_params marked do_remote_decode, so P runs only the prefill.

P prefills, keeps the 128 blocks pinned under a lease (kv_lease_duration, default 30 s) and returns kv_transfer_params: its block ids, engine id, host and port. The proxy keeps only these; D streams every output token.

The proxy forwards the request and those parameters to a decoder. On first contact D and P exchange NIXL agent metadata over the side channel. D allocates local blocks and starts heartbeats that extend P's lease while the request waits.
When D schedules the request it posts one-sided RDMA reads of P's registered blocks into its own. P's GPU and CPU do no work for the copy: this is a pull.

add.label: KV bytes, no P CPU work

scenes.caption: D notifies P that the read finished, and P frees the blocks at once instead of waiting for the lease to run out.
D adds the request to its decode batch and streams tokens back through the proxy.

blocks.md:
Three pieces make the one-sided read possible.

- **Memory registration**: each engine registers its KV pool with the network card through NIXL and its UCX backend, so the card may read or write it directly. The *RDMA* course (not a prerequisite) explains registration, keys and one-sided READ and WRITE.
- **A side channel**: before the first read, D and P exchange NIXL agent metadata, which describes each side's registered memory, over an ordinary socket on `VLLM_NIXL_SIDE_CHANNEL_PORT` (default 5600).
- **Descriptor lists**: a transfer is posted as a list of memory regions. vLLM's transfer metrics report the average number of descriptors per transfer, because fragmented allocations need more of them and make posting slower.

**Pull or push.** In vLLM's default `NixlPullConnector` (alias `NixlConnector`) D reads when it is ready, so D controls timing and memory while P holds the blocks. [`NixlPushConnector`](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/design/nixl_kv_push_connector/) reverses it: D pre-allocates blocks and registers them with P, and P writes straight into D's GPU memory once both the registration and the finished blocks are present. The two protocols are incompatible and are never paired. Splitwise pushes too: its prompt machine sends each layer's KV over InfiniBand with a zero-copy one-sided put from MSCCL++ (a GPU-driven communication library), with no receive call on the token machine, then signals a semaphore the token machine waits on. Mooncake pushes each layer into the decode node's CPU memory, and SGLang's decode server by default pre-allocates KV and signals the prefill server to start (a `prefill_complete` allocation policy defers that until prefill finishes).

blocks.prompt: Push lets the transfer overlap the prefill layer by layer. What must a push design decide before the prefill starts that a pull design can leave until later, and what does pull pay instead?
blocks.reveal: Push needs the **destination**: which decode node, and memory already allocated there. Splitwise picks both machines when it schedules the request, and SGLang's decode server pre-allocates before prefill begins. Pull can choose and admit later, when a decode slot is actually free (DistServe's decode side pulls when it has room, so prefill memory absorbs bursts, lesson 3). The price of pull is that P must keep the blocks, under a lease, until someone reads them, and a decoder that never comes leaves memory stranded until the lease ends.

blocks.md: **Different parallelism on each side.** Lesson 3 argued each phase should get its own parallelism, so P may run TP=4 while D runs TP=2. Tensor parallelism splits attention by heads, and each rank stores the KV of its own heads only. Llama 3 8B has 8 KV heads, so a P rank holds 2 and a D rank needs 4: every D rank gathers from two P ranks, and each P block must land in the right part of a D block. vLLM works out this mapping once per remote engine at handshake time, in [`tp_mapping.py`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/nixl/tp_mapping.py).

blocks.title: Which prefill ranks each decode rank reads

scenes.caption: Llama 3 8B has 8 KV heads. Prefill runs TP=4, so each P rank stores 2 heads; decode runs TP=2, so each D rank needs 4.
D rank 0 needs heads 0 to 3, held by P ranks 0 and 1: for every block, two reads of 512 KiB (2 heads x K and V x 32 layers x 128 x 2 bytes x 16 tokens).
D rank 1 reads P ranks 2 and 3. A 128-block request costs 256 reads per D rank, against 128 if prefill also ran TP=2.
Reverse it: P TP=2, D TP=4. D rank 1 needs heads 2 and 3, the second half of P rank 0's four. It reads a slice of each P block, one contiguous range only if the block stores heads outermost.

blocks.code:
# Which prefill ranks each decode rank reads, for 8 KV heads (Llama 3 8B),
# following the head split in vLLM's NIXL tp_mapping.py (GQA, head-major layout)
HEADS, LAYERS, HEAD_DIM, BLOCK = 8, 32, 128, 16
def heads_of(rank, tp):               # KV heads stored on one rank
    return list(range(rank * HEADS // tp, (rank + 1) * HEADS // tp))
def plan(p_tp, d_tp, prompt):
    blocks = -(-prompt // BLOCK)
    print(f"P TP{p_tp} to D TP{d_tp}, {prompt} tokens = {blocks} blocks")
    for d in range(d_tp):
        mine = set(heads_of(d, d_tp))
        src = [p for p in range(p_tp) if mine & set(heads_of(p, p_tp))]
        per_read = len(mine & set(heads_of(src[0], p_tp))) * 2 * LAYERS * HEAD_DIM * 2 * BLOCK
        print(f"  D rank {d} heads {sorted(mine)} reads P ranks {src}: "
              f"{blocks * len(src)} block reads of {per_read // 1024} KiB")
plan(4, 2, 2048)
plan(2, 4, 2048)
blocks.caption: hetero.py: which P ranks each D rank reads, in both directions, with the head split vLLM uses for GQA models.

blocks.md:
Output:

```
P TP4 to D TP2, 2048 tokens = 128 blocks
  D rank 0 heads [0, 1, 2, 3] reads P ranks [0, 1]: 256 block reads of 512 KiB
  D rank 1 heads [4, 5, 6, 7] reads P ranks [2, 3]: 256 block reads of 512 KiB
P TP2 to D TP4, 2048 tokens = 128 blocks
  D rank 0 heads [0, 1] reads P ranks [0]: 128 block reads of 512 KiB
  D rank 1 heads [2, 3] reads P ranks [0]: 128 block reads of 512 KiB
  D rank 2 heads [4, 5] reads P ranks [1]: 128 block reads of 512 KiB
  D rank 3 heads [6, 7] reads P ranks [1]: 128 block reads of 512 KiB
```

Going from TP4 to TP2 doubles the reads per D rank; going from TP2 to TP4 keeps one source rank but reads half of each of its blocks. These are logical block reads: with the default layout vLLM registers each layer's cache as its own region (an optional cross-layer `BLHNC` layout packs all layers of a block together) and posts one descriptor per region and block, so real descriptor counts are a multiple of these, in the same ratio.

Whether that half is contiguous depends on the **KV layout** inside a block. vLLM's docs call the head-major layout LBHNC (formerly HND: heads outside tokens) and the token-major one LBNHC (formerly NHD). The connector defaults to head-major for transfer performance; token-major works but cannot split heads across ranks, and an experimental `enable_permute_local_kv` option converts between them. Block sizes may also differ (with pull, prefill blocks may be smaller than decode blocks, not larger), while model, KV dtype and attention backend must match: a compatibility hash checked at handshake rejects a mismatched pair. MLA models such as DeepSeek-V3 keep the same compressed KV on every TP rank, so a D rank reads from a single P rank.

**When the decoder is late.** P cannot keep blocks forever, and it must not free them early. vLLM first used one fixed timeout (480 s by default): a crashed decoder left gigabytes of dead blocks on P for up to 8 minutes, while a shorter timeout freed blocks during traffic surges before an overloaded decoder could read them, wasting the prefill. The current design is a **lease**. P pins the blocks for `kv_lease_duration` (default 30 s). From the moment the request enters D's scheduler, D sends a heartbeat about every 5 s (a sixth of the lease), each extending the lease by about 20 s (two thirds). A read-done notification frees the blocks at once. Heartbeats ride on NIXL's notification channel, and one batched message to a prefiller renews all of that decoder's requests there.

blocks.title: A KV lease on the prefiller: three cases

scenes.caption: Prefill ends at 0 s. The request enters D's queue at 1 s and waits 41 s behind other work. D heartbeats about every 5 s, each extending the lease about 20 s, so the blocks survive past the initial 30 s; the read at 42 s frees them.
D crashes at 27 s. Its last heartbeat, at 26 s, keeps the lease alive until about 46 s, so P reclaims the blocks within seconds of the lease end, not after the 8 minutes of the old fixed timeout.

A router holds the request outside D for 35 s, so no heartbeats go out. The lease ends at 30 s and P reuses the blocks. Before reading, D compares P's exported deadline with its clock (5 s margin) and declines; kv_load_failure_policy decides the rest.

blocks.md: **What a failed load does.** `kv_load_failure_policy` decides: `fail`, the default, ends the request with an error; `recompute` makes D prefill the missing blocks itself. The docs warn that recompute runs prefill on a decode-tuned instance and brings back the interference this course started with, so it is a fallback, not a plan. Without it, though, every lost transfer becomes a user-visible error. Counters to watch: `vllm:nixl_num_kv_expired_reqs` on P (leases that ran out: the lease is too short or decode is overloaded), `vllm:nixl_num_declined_expired_reads` on the reader, `vllm:nixl_num_failed_transfers`, and `vllm:nixl_num_notifications_after_expiry`, which in pull mode means D may have read blocks that were already reused.

A successful RDMA read proves nothing about the data. If P's lease ran out and the blocks were recycled for another prompt, the read still completes and returns that other request's KV; the symptom is corrupted output or NaN logits, not a transport error. That is why vLLM's decoder checks the lease deadline P exported, rebased with a clock offset measured at handshake, before the read and again when it completes.

**Research view: replicate the KV.** DéjàVu (Strati et al., 2024) builds a KV streaming library and uses it for prompt-token disaggregation, for swapping micro-batches out of GPU memory, and for fault tolerance. For the last, each pipeline stage streams its KV cache to the next stage as tokens are generated, a controller detects failures from missed heartbeats, and recovery copies the replica back and resumes from the last replicated step instead of recomputing the prompt and every token so far. The price is extra network traffic on every step; the payoff is losing a few steps of work instead of whole requests.

The handoff is a small distributed protocol: metadata through the proxy, one-sided reads of registered memory, a lease kept alive by the consumer's heartbeats, and a failure policy on the consumer. Different parallelism on the two sides multiplies the reads and needs a layout in which each rank's heads are contiguous.

blocks.question: A decoder issues its RDMA read 40 s after P finished the prefill. A router held the request the whole time, so D never sent a heartbeat. What can go wrong, and how does vLLM's pull connector catch it?
options: Nothing: a read of freed memory fails with a transport error, so stale data is never used
P extends the lease by itself while blocks are unread, so the read is safe
The read can succeed on blocks P already reused for another prompt; D checks P's exported lease deadline before and after the read, declines it, and applies kv_load_failure_policy
D detects it by checksumming the received KV against the prompt tokens
blocks.explain: Only heartbeats from D, sent once the request is in D's scheduler, extend the 30 s lease. Held outside D, the lease expired and P recycled the blocks. NIXL would happily read them and return another request's KV. The connector checks whether P's deadline, rebased to its own clock, falls within a 5 s safety margin of now, declines the read, counts it in vllm:nixl_num_declined_expired_reads, and follows the failure policy.

blocks.question: Prefill runs TP=4 and decode TP=2 for a model with 8 KV heads and head-major KV blocks. For a 128-block request, how many block reads does each decode rank issue?
options: 128, one per block, as with equal TP
256: each D rank needs 4 heads held by 2 P ranks, so 2 reads per block
512: every D rank reads every P rank
64, because a D block holds two P blocks
blocks.explain: A D rank's 4 heads are split over 2 P ranks (2 heads each), so it reads 2 slices per block: 2 x 128 = 256. Reading every P rank would fetch heads the D rank does not own; block counts do not change with TP, only the heads per block slice.

lessons.title: Chunked prefill or disaggregation: when each one wins

blocks.md:
Disaggregation is not the only fix for interference. **Sarathi-Serve** (Agrawal et al., OSDI 2024) keeps both phases on the same GPUs and changes how batches are built:

- **Chunked prefill**: split a long prompt into chunks processed over several iterations.
- **Stall-free batching**: each iteration first packs every running decode, then fills the remaining **token budget** with prefill chunks, so decodes never wait for a whole prompt.

The budget is chosen from the TBT SLO by profiling: the largest number of tokens per iteration that still meets it.

Why is this cheap? Decode iterations are memory-bound, so they leave arithmetic idle. A prefill chunk of a few hundred tokens fills that slack. Sarathi-Serve reports up to 2.6x higher serving capacity than vLLM for Mistral-7B on one A100 and up to 3.7x for Yi-34B on two A100s. The figure replays lesson 1's arrival with three designs, using the same made-up cost model.

blocks.title: Prompt C arrives at 30 ms: three designs

scenes.caption: Colocated, full prefill (lesson 1): the 16 running requests wait 104 ms for one token. C's TTFT is 110.4 ms.
Chunked, budget 256: each iteration holds 16 decodes plus a 240-token chunk and costs 25.6 ms. Decodes see 25.6 ms gaps instead of a 104 ms stall; C's TTFT grows to 127.0 ms.
Disaggregated: C's prefill runs alone on its own GPU (TTFT 102.4 ms), its KV moves in 5.4 ms (1024 tokens at 50 GB/s), and decode steps never change from 18.2 ms. C joins the batch at 145.6 ms.

blocks.md: Chunking has costs. It is not unique to Sarathi-Serve: DeepSpeed-MII, Microsoft's DeepSpeed Model Implementations for Inference library, also splits prompts into chunks, and DistServe uses it as its chunked-prefill baseline. DistServe argues it only mitigates interference: small chunks underuse the GPU and stretch TTFT, large chunks leave little room for decodes, and every chunk must re-read the KV cache of all earlier chunks. Sarathi-Serve agrees the extra reads exist but finds attention prefill stays compute-bound even at small chunk sizes, so the overhead is small in practice. The hard part is picking the budget: the vLLM docs say chunked prefill with a proper chunk size can control tail ITL too, "but in practice it's hard to figure out the correct chunk size value".

blocks.title: Toy simulation: per-GPU goodput, chunked vs disaggregated

scenes.caption: Same toy workload and simulator as lessons 2 and 3 (1024-token prompts, 128 output tokens, SLOs 400 ms and 25 ms). A budget of 128 is too small for TTFT; 512 is too large for TPOT.

Tuned well (192 to 256), one chunked GPU reaches about 6 req/s, above the best disaggregated ratio's 5.12 per GPU. Simplified: the toy charges nothing for chunking, uses short prompts, and gives disaggregation no per-phase parallelism or hardware edge.

blocks.prompt: The toy shows chunked prefill beating disaggregation, yet DistServe reports up to 7.4x more requests (or 12.6x tighter SLOs) than vLLM and its chunked-prefill baseline DeepSpeed-MII. What does the toy leave out that the paper exploits?
blocks.reveal: The toy gives every design identical 1-GPU instances. DistServe's wins come largely from **choosing different parallelism and GPU counts per phase** (for example tensor parallelism for a tight TTFT), from **long prompts** where chunks multiply KV reloads and decode stalls, and from **tight SLOs on both metrics at once**. Splitwise adds **different hardware per phase**. The toy is honest about one thing: on a small model with short prompts, a well-tuned colocated scheduler is a strong baseline.

blocks.md:
How the sources draw the line:

- **Disaggregation tends to win** with long prompts, strict TTFT and TPOT SLOs together, large models that need different parallelism per phase, enough GPUs to size pools, and a fast KV fabric (NVLink or RDMA). DistServe also argues long context helps: prefill compute grows faster than KV size.
- **Colocation (with chunked prefill) tends to win** for throughput-oriented offline jobs, few GPUs, small models, short prompts, or slow interconnects. DistServe's own discussion says chunked prefill may be preferred in offline settings, and simpler non-disaggregated systems in resource-constrained ones.

The vLLM docs add one more note: disaggregated prefill "DOES NOT improve throughput". Its point is controlling TTFT and tail ITL separately.

Production systems blur the line. NVIDIA **Dynamo** runs workers from vLLM, SGLang or TensorRT-LLM (three serving engines) in separate prefill and decode pools, moves KV with NIXL, and its docs state disaggregation "is not automatically better": for small models, short prompts, low concurrency or no fast KV-transfer fabric, aggregated (colocated) serving is simpler and often faster.

Its experimental **conditional disaggregation** sends a request to remote prefill only when needed. The router computes the **effective input length**: the prompt minus the prefix already cached on the chosen decode worker. Under the isl_bounding policy (isl stands for input sequence length), if that is short enough (default threshold 2048 tokens) and also a small enough share of the full prompt (effective over full length below a ratio threshold, default 0.7), the decode worker prefills it locally. Mooncake similarly chunks very long prefills and splits them across prefill nodes.

**A worked decision.** Put lessons 2 to 5 together on one case: Llama 3 70B in BF16 (80 layers, model width 8192, 8 KV heads of 128, from the Llama 3 paper), 8,192-token prompts, 300 output tokens, SLOs of TTFT 2 s and TPOT 50 ms at 90% attainment, and 16 H100-80GB GPUs in two 8-GPU nodes, NVLink inside a node and 400 Gb/s between nodes. Assumptions, all in the code: 400 TFLOP/s sustained per GPU (about 40% of the H100's 989 TFLOP/s dense BF16 peak, the rate lesson 4 assumed), the full 3.35 TB/s of HBM bandwidth, TP=4 instances (140 GB of weights need at least two GPUs; four leave room for KV), and no cost for tensor-parallel communication.

blocks.code:
# Llama 3 70B in BF16 on H100-80GB GPUs, TP4 instances, 8K prompts, 300 outputs
L, KVH, HD, DQ, N = 80, 8, 128, 8192, 70e9     # layers, KV heads, head dim, query width
PROMPT, OUT, TP = 8192, 300, 4
FLOPS, BW, HBM, LINK = 400e12, 3.35e12, 80e9, 50e9  # per GPU; 400 Gb/s between nodes
kv_tok = 2 * L * KVH * HD * 2
kv_req = PROMPT * kv_tok
pf_flop = 2 * N * PROMPT + 2 * PROMPT**2 * DQ * L   # weights + causal attention
ctx = PROMPT + OUT / 2                              # mean context while decoding
dec_flop = 2 * N + 4 * ctx * DQ * L                 # per decode token
room = TP * 0.9 * HBM - 2 * N                       # keep 10% for activations
if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(f"KV: {kv_tok // 1024} KiB/token, {kv_req / 2**30:.2f} GiB per request")
    print(f"prefill: {pf_flop / 1e12:.0f} TFLOP, {pf_flop / (TP * FLOPS):.3f} s on TP{TP}")
    print(f"cross-node KV copy: {kv_req / LINK * 1e3:.1f} ms per request")
    print(f"decode TP{TP}: {room / 1e9:.0f} GB for KV, "
          f"{room / ((PROMPT + OUT) * kv_tok):.0f} full-length requests")

```
KV: 320 KiB/token, 2.50 GiB per request
prefill: 1235 TFLOP, 0.772 s on TP4
cross-node KV copy: 53.7 ms per request
decode TP4: 148 GB for KV, 53 full-length requests
```

One prefill occupies a TP4 instance for 0.77 s, so an instance prefills at most about 1.3 requests/s. The cross-node copy adds 54 ms, small against a 2 s TTFT. Now plug a TP4 cost into lesson 2's simulator and compare four colocated instances with three prefill instances and one decode instance (3P1D: two prefill instances in node 1, the third with the decoder in node 2).

blocks.code:
import goodput_sim as g, designs as d
from size70b import *

def cost(P, B):           # one TP4 instance: P prefill tokens, B decodes
    P = P + 128 if P else 0                         # per-chunk overhead
    mem = (2 * N + B * ctx * kv_tok) / (TP * BW)
    math = (P * pf_flop / PROMPT + B * dec_flop) / (TP * FLOPS)
    return max(mem, math)

g.cost, d.PROMPT, d.OUT, d.SLO_TTFT = cost, PROMPT, OUT, 2.0
arr0 = d.arrivals
d.arrivals = lambda rate: arr0(rate, n=600)

def colo4(rate, budget=None):     # 4 colocated TP4 instances, round-robin
    arr, res = d.arrivals(rate * 4), {}
    for k in range(4):
        ids = range(k, len(arr), 4)
        f, e = g.gpu([[arr[i], PROMPT, OUT - 1] for i in ids], budget)
        res.update({i: (f[j] - arr[i], (e[j] - f[j]) / (OUT - 1))
                    for j, i in enumerate(ids)})
    return [res[i] for i in range(len(arr))]

for tpot in (0.050, 0.015):
    d.SLO_TPOT = tpot
    gp = lambda f: d.goodput(f, hi=2) * 4           # requests/s on 16 GPUs
    print(f"TPOT SLO {tpot * 1e3:.0f} ms, goodput of the 16 GPUs (req/s):")
    print(f"  colocated, no chunking {gp(colo4):.2f}")
    for b in (256, 512, 1024):
        print(f"  colocated, chunk {b:4d}  {gp(lambda r: colo4(r, b)):.2f}")
    print(f"  3P1D                   {gp(lambda r: d.disagg(r, 3, 1, kv_req / LINK)):.2f}")

Every 3P1D request pays the 54 ms copy (pessimistic).

```
TPOT SLO 50 ms, goodput of the 16 GPUs (req/s):
  colocated, no chunking 3.45
  colocated, chunk  256  2.47
  colocated, chunk  512  3.20
  colocated, chunk 1024  3.40
  3P1D                   2.97
TPOT SLO 15 ms, goodput of the 16 GPUs (req/s):
  colocated, no chunking 0.96
  colocated, chunk  256  0.91
  colocated, chunk  512  0.94
  colocated, chunk 1024  0.95
  3P1D                   2.97
```

In this simulation, with a 50 ms TPOT SLO, plain colocation wins (3.45 against 2.97 req/s). The workload is prefill-heavy, and the split must give a quarter of the GPUs to decode, where they idle: at 2.97 req/s the decoder runs about 11 requests in a 12.8 ms step, with room for 53. TPOT is an average, so a 0.77 s stall spread over 300 tokens costs only 2.6 ms each. At 15 ms every colocated variant falls below 1 req/s while 3P1D keeps 2.97, because its decode steps never carry prefill. Bandwidth is no issue: 2.97 x 2/3 x 2.68 GB is 5.3 GB/s across the node boundary, against 50 GB/s.

An averaged TPOT SLO hides stalls. The simulated colocated win at 50 ms holds for that SLO, yet its users see a 0.77 s freeze whenever a prompt lands in their batch. If the product needs a bound on the worst gap, write it as a p99 ITL SLO and rerun: that stall is exactly what disaggregation removes.

blocks.question: In the worked decision with a 15 ms TPOT SLO, 3P1D keeps 2.97 req/s while every colocated variant drops below 1. Why?
options: Disaggregation needs fewer FLOPs per request
The 400 Gb/s link is faster than NVLink
Colocated instances run out of KV memory first
Its decode steps (about 13 ms) never include prefill tokens, while any colocated step that carries a prompt or a chunk runs past 15 ms
blocks.explain: Total work is the same either way. A colocated TP4 step with even 256 prefill tokens plus the 128-token overhead costs about 36 ms of math, and a whole prompt 0.77 s, so TPOT misses pile up. The decode instance's steps are weight and KV reads only, about 12.8 ms at its load, so 15 ms holds. Memory is far from full (11 of 53 slots), and the link is slower than NVLink, not faster.

blocks.md: Disaggregation adds failure modes. DistServe notes a fault in one decode instance that serves several prefill instances can spread, and FCFS prefill can create a convoy effect where long prompts block short ones. Mooncake must sometimes reject a request after its prefill if no decode slot is left, wasting that prefill. Lesson 5 covers leases, lost transfers and failure policies.

Chunked prefill bounds interference inside one GPU; disaggregation removes it and lets each phase get its own hardware, parallelism and scale. Pick by measuring per-GPU goodput under your SLOs, prompt lengths and interconnect, not by architecture preference.

blocks.question: An offline batch job summarizes millions of documents overnight. There is no latency SLO; the goal is tokens per dollar. Which design do the sources point toward?
options: Separate prefill and decode clusters on different GPU generations, mandatory for throughput
Colocated serving with chunked prefill to keep every iteration near the compute-bound point
Disaggregation over 25 Gb/s Ethernet to save NVLink
Disaggregation, because it always raises goodput
blocks.explain: Goodput only matters when there are SLOs. DistServe's discussion says that in throughput-oriented offline settings, chunked prefill with piggybacking (decode tokens riding along in the batch of each prefill chunk) may be preferred because it fills each batch to the compute-bound threshold. vLLM's docs also note disaggregated prefill does not improve throughput.

blocks.question: Under Dynamo's conditional disaggregation (isl_bounding policy, default threshold 2048 tokens), a 6000-token chat turn arrives and 5000 of its tokens are already cached on the chosen decode worker. Assuming the ratio condition also passes, where is it prefilled?
options: On the decode worker itself, since only about 1000 uncached tokens remain
On a remote prefill worker, because 6000 exceeds 2048
It is rejected
It is split between both pools
blocks.explain: The policy looks at effective input length: the prompt minus the cached prefix overlap on the selected decode worker, here 1000 tokens, below the 2048 default. The decode worker prefills locally, saving a KV transfer and remote prefill work. The default ratio threshold is 0.7, and 1000/6000 is about 0.17, so the ratio check passes too.

lessons.title: Disaggregation at scale: MoE, expert parallelism and elastic pools

blocks.md: DistServe, Splitwise and most of this course's numbers come from dense models. The largest deployments today serve **mixture-of-experts** (MoE) models, where each token runs through a few of many expert MLPs, and there disaggregation became the standard layout. **Expert parallelism** (EP) spreads the experts over many GPUs, and each MoE layer sends tokens to their experts and back with two all-to-all exchanges (every GPU sends to every other), called dispatch and combine. This lesson covers why MoE pushed the phases apart, how pools are resized as traffic shifts, and the next split inside decode.

DeepSeek-V3 (671B parameters, 37B active per token, 256 routed experts with 8 chosen per token plus 1 shared expert) is served on H800 nodes (a Hopper GPU like the H100, with lower NVLink bandwidth: 160 GB/s in DeepSeek's report) with prefill and decode separated. Its report sizes the two units very differently: prefill uses 4 nodes (32 GPUs) with EP32, and decode 40 nodes (320 GPUs) with EP320. Both keep **redundant experts**, extra copies of the most loaded experts, re-chosen from live statistics (for prefill about every 10 minutes), so every GPU gets a similar number of tokens.

scenes.caption: Prefill unit: 4 nodes, 32 GPUs. Attention runs TP4 in 8 data-parallel groups; each GPU hosts 8 of the 256 routed experts plus 1 redundant copy of a hot one. Two micro-batches overlap one's compute with the other's all-to-all.
The prompt's KV cache moves to the decode unit, as in lessons 4 and 5.
Decode unit: 40 nodes, 320 GPUs. Attention TP4 x DP80; each GPU hosts one expert, and 64 GPUs hold redundant and shared experts. Dispatch and combine go point to point over InfiniBand.
Two shapes for two phases: the decode unit is 10 times wider so each expert sees enough tokens per step. A colocated deployment would have to pick one shape for both.

blocks.code:
# DeepSeek-V3 MoE layers: 256 routed experts, top-8, hidden 7168, expert width 2048
E, K, H, F, MOE_LAYERS = 256, 8, 7168, 2048, 58
expert_bytes = 3 * H * F * MOE_LAYERS          # FP8: one byte per weight, all layers
for phase, tok_per_gpu, G in [("prefill", 4096, 32), ("decode", 64, 32),
                              ("decode", 64, 320)]:
    per_expert = tok_per_gpu * G * K / E       # average tokens an expert gets
    experts_per_gpu = max(E / G, 1)
    print(f"{phase:7s} EP{G:<3d} {tok_per_gpu:5d} tok/GPU: {per_expert:6.0f} tok/expert, "
          f"{experts_per_gpu:4.0f} experts/GPU = {experts_per_gpu*expert_bytes/1e9:5.1f} GB")

Output:

```
prefill EP32   4096 tok/GPU:   4096 tok/expert,    8 experts/GPU =  20.4 GB
decode  EP32     64 tok/GPU:     64 tok/expert,    8 experts/GPU =  20.4 GB
decode  EP320    64 tok/GPU:    640 tok/expert,    1 experts/GPU =   2.6 GB
```

With $B$ tokens per step, each expert gets $8B/256 = B/32$ tokens on average (each token picks 8 of the 256 experts), and its matrix multiplies stay memory-bound until that count reaches a few hundred. A prefill GPU brings thousands of tokens, so EP32 is plenty. A decode GPU brings only its batch of sequences, one token each, so widening EP is the way to feed each expert: 10 times the GPUs, 10 times the tokens per expert, and one expert per GPU frees about 18 GB of HBM for KV and larger batches. DeepSeek's report notes its per-expert decode batch is usually within 256 tokens, so real batches are smaller than this example; the trend is the point.

SGLang reproduced this design on 12 nodes of 8 H100s (96 GPUs) and published its measurements (not run here): about 52.3k input and 22.3k output tokens per second per node for 2,000-token inputs. Prefill on 4 nodes with EP32 reached 57,674, 54,543 and 50,302 tokens/s per node for 1K, 2K and 4K prompts; decode on 9 nodes with EP72 reached 22,282 tokens/s per node at 2K context, 5.2x its TP16 baseline, a gain the team attributes mostly to the 4x larger batches EP allows by cutting per-GPU weight memory. The two phases were benchmarked separately (4 + 9 nodes exceeds the 12). They also list why a unified engine fails here: prefill batches interrupt decode, data-parallel attention ranks (each GPU runs attention for its own requests) end up mixing phases, and the two all-to-all modes of DeepEP (DeepSeek's open-source expert-parallel communication library) (normal for prefill, low-latency for decode) cannot both run in one communication group. Expert load also differs between the phases, so each pool gets its own expert placement.

**Keeping the ratio right.** Lesson 3 found the best pool ratio by search; a back-of-envelope version is each phase's share of GPU time. With lesson 1's toy costs a prompt of $L_p$ tokens takes $0.1L_p$ ms of prefill GPU time, and a decode GPU at the 25 ms TPOT limit runs 50 requests per step ($15 + 0.2B \le 25$), so each output token costs $25/50 = 0.5$ ms of decode GPU time. The prefill share is $0.1L_p / (0.1L_p + 0.5L_o)$ for $L_o$ output tokens.

blocks.code:
# Toy cost model: prefill costs 0.1 ms per prompt token; a decode GPU holds the
# largest batch that meets TPOT 25 ms: 15 + 0.2 B <= 25, so B = 50 at 25 ms/step
def p_share(prompt, out):
    prefill = 0.1 * prompt              # GPU-ms per request
    decode = out * 25 / 50              # GPU-ms per request (25 ms step shared by 50)
    return prefill / (prefill + decode)
GPUS = 6
for hours, prompt, out in [("00-08", 1024, 256), ("08-14", 4096, 128),
                           ("14-20", 2048, 256), ("20-24", 1024, 512)]:
    s = p_share(prompt, out)
    print(f"{hours}: prompt {prompt:4d}, output {out:3d}: P share {s:.2f}, "
          f"{GPUS*s:.2f} of {GPUS} GPUs, so {round(GPUS*s)}P{GPUS-round(GPUS*s)}D")
print("check, toy workload (1024 in, 128 out):", round(p_share(1024, 128) / (1 - p_share(1024, 128)), 2), ": 1")

blocks.title: Six GPUs over one day: fixed split vs elastic pools

scenes.caption: A fixed 4P2D split, right for the afternoon mix (2,048 in, 256 out). From 08 to 14, when long documents arrive (4,096 in, 128 out), the formula wants 5.2 prefill GPUs; at night (1,024 in, 512 out) only 1.7. Made-up traffic, script-computed ratios.

Following the formula: 3P3D, then 5P1D, 4P2D and 2P4D. Each switch drains a GPU and flips its role; TetriInfer measured the flip itself at 5 to 7 ms, excluding the drain. A real planner also needs headroom and must not flip on every blip.

blocks.md:
Systems that follow the mix:

- **TetriInfer** (Hu et al., 2024) predicts each request's output-length bucket with a small model (OPT-125M for OPT-13B), places decodes to avoid hotspots of long generations, and **flips** idle instances between prefill and decode within fixed hardware, for example when an instance has run under 10% load for a minute.
- **Splitwise**'s mixed pool (lesson 3) borrows machines from either pool when queues grow.
- **NVIDIA Dynamo's Planner** scales prefill and decode workers separately: its load-based mode watches prefill queue tokens and decode KV-cache utilization every few seconds, and its SLA mode predicts traffic and sizes pools to TTFT and ITL targets, because a new GPU worker takes minutes to start.
- **llm-d** packages the same pieces for Kubernetes: vLLM with NixlConnector RDMA, wide EP, and autoscaling.

Scaling or admitting on the current load of the other pool oscillates. Mooncake saw it with early rejection: decode looks idle, so many requests are admitted; they reach decode one prefill later, decode looks full, so admissions stop and prefill idles, and the cycle repeats in opposite phase. Its fix was to decide on the decode load predicted for when the request will arrive there.

**The next split: attention and FFN.** Inside decode, two kinds of work still share each GPU. Attention is stateful: each request reads its own KV cache, so it is memory-bound and grows with context. The FFN or experts are stateless weights shared by every token and want large batches. **Attention-FFN disaggregation** puts them on different GPUs and ships hidden states between them twice per layer. MegaScale-Infer (Zhu et al., ByteDance Seed) does this for MoE decode, with attention nodes replicated to gather a large batch for each expert node, a custom M2N communication library (M attention nodes sending to N expert nodes), and a **ping-pong pipeline** of micro-batches so each side computes while the other's results travel. Its motivating example: a batch of 156 with 2 of 8 experts per token gives each expert 39 tokens, a theoretical FFN utilization of 25%.

blocks.tex: T_f = \max(T_a, T_e),\qquad T_a \approx T_e,\qquad T_c < T_f,\qquad m \times T_f \ge 2\,(T_f + T_c)
blocks.caption: MegaScale-Infer's conditions for m micro-batches: balance attention (T_a) and expert (T_e) compute, keep one transfer (T_c) shorter than a compute stage, and use enough micro-batches that the others' work covers one micro-batch's round trip of two computes and two transfers.

blocks.title: Ping-pong micro-batches between attention and FFN GPUs

scenes.caption: Two micro-batches, two layers; compute takes 2 ms per stage and each one-way transfer 1 ms (made-up). After m1 and m2 finish attention, the attention GPUs wait 2 ms for m1 to return: busy 4 ms of every 6 (67%), since m x Tf = 4 is less than 2(Tf + Tc) = 6.

Three micro-batches meet the condition exactly (6 = 6): m1 returns just as m3 finishes, so attention runs back to back and the FFN GPUs, after the first 3 ms, stay busy too. Same compute, more work in flight.

blocks.md: MegaScale-Infer reports up to 1.90x higher per-GPU decode throughput than state-of-the-art systems. Step-3 (StepFun) designs a 321B model around the same split, with a 3-stage pipeline of attention, FFN and communication at 16.6 ms each for a 50 ms TPOT, and reports up to 4,039 output tokens/s per Hopper GPU (its best minute; 3,910 on average) at 4K context, FP8 and no multi-token prediction (DeepSeek-V3's extra module that proposes further tokens for speculative decoding). It compares that with 2,324 for DeepSeek-V3, a number DeepSeek published from its own profiling under the same 20 tokens/s target, so the two come from different teams' runs.

At scale, disaggregation is about shapes: prefill and decode want different expert-parallel widths, communication modes and batch sizes, and their best ratio moves with the traffic mix. Size pools from each phase's share of GPU time, resize on predicted rather than current load, and expect decode itself to split further into attention and FFN.

blocks.question: After a product launch, prompts get 4x longer while output lengths stay the same. In a disaggregated deployment with a load-based autoscaler, which pool should grow, and which signal moves first?
options: Decode, first seen as rising TPOT
Neither: the P:D ratio depends only on the request rate
Prefill, first seen as queued prefill tokens and rising TTFT; decode KV utilization climbs later as the larger caches arrive
Both equally, first seen as GPU utilization
blocks.explain: Prefill work per request grows at least 4x (more with attention), so the prefill share of GPU time rises, as in the 08 to 14 window of the timeline. Requests queue at prefill before anything reaches decode, so queued prefill tokens and TTFT move first, the signal Dynamo's load-based planner watches. Each request also brings 4x more KV, so decode KV-cache utilization rises next and decode may need capacity too.

blocks.question: Why does DeepSeek-V3's decode unit use EP320 when its prefill unit gets by with EP32?
options: A decode step has few tokens per GPU, so only a wide EP group gives each expert enough tokens, and one expert per GPU frees HBM for KV and larger batches
Decode does more FLOPs per token than prefill
The KV cache must be split across experts
Wider EP removes the all-to-all exchanges
blocks.explain: Tokens per expert per step are B/32 for B tokens in the EP group. Prefill GPUs bring thousands of tokens each, decode GPUs only their batch. Widening the group multiplies the tokens each expert sees and shrinks expert weights per GPU (20.4 GB to 2.6 GB in the script), leaving memory for KV. All-to-all remains; it just goes point to point.

blocks.question: In a ping-pong pipeline, attention and FFN each take 2 ms per micro-batch and a one-way transfer takes 1 ms. What is the smallest number of micro-batches that keeps both sides busy?
blocks.explain: The condition is m x Tf at least 2(Tf + Tc): 2m at least 6, so m = 3. With 2, the attention GPUs idle 2 ms per layer waiting for a micro-batch to come back, as in the first scene of the timeline. More micro-batches also work but shrink each one, which lowers the per-expert batch.
